title: while & do-while
summary: Learn pre-test while loops for event-driven iteration and post-test do-while loops for guaranteed first execution.
learningObjectives: Master while & do-while concepts and syntax in Java
Trace variable state transformations across iterations
Avoid common infinite loop and off-by-one errors
expectedOutcomes: Write bug-free loops using while & do-while
Select appropriate loop structures based on problem requirements

activities.title: Core Concept: while & do-while

breakdown.whatIsIt: while & do-while enables repeating blocks of code efficiently based on termination criteria.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Automation of repetitive tasks is the foundational superpower of computers.
howItWorks: Evaluate loop continuation condition before each pass
Execute body statements if condition is true
Update loop state and re-evaluate condition until false
keyTakeaways: Every loop requires a reachable termination condition to avoid infinite looping
Variables declared inside a loop body exist only for that specific iteration
Choose the loop type that best matches your problem constraints

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: while & do-while
activities.description:
Lines 4-8: counter starts at 10. while (counter < 5) tests 10 < 5 (false). Body is skipped completely.
Lines 12-16: do block executes unconditionally, printing 'do-while body executed at least once!'.
Line 16: while (counter < 5) tests 11 < 5 (false), terminating the loop.
This clearly demonstrates that do-while guarantees at least 1 execution.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of times a while loop body can execute?
questions.explanation: Because a while loop evaluates its condition before entering the body, if the condition is initially false, it executes 0 times.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of times a do-while loop body can execute?
questions.explanation: A do-while loop executes its body first before evaluating the condition at the end, guaranteeing at least 1 execution.

questions.prompt: Which loop structure requires a terminating semicolon `;` after the closing parenthesis of its condition?
questions.explanation: In Java, a do-while statement must end with a semicolon: `do { ... } while (condition);`. Omitting it causes a syntax error.
Pass 1: prints 1, x becomes 2. 2 <= 3 is true. Pass 2: prints 2, x becomes 3. 3 <= 3 is true. Pass 3: prints 3, x becomes 4. 4 <= 3 is false. Output: '1 2 3 '.

questions.prompt: Why is do-while the standard choice for user input validation loops?
options: Because do-while runs 2x faster than while
Because input must be requested at least once before testing if it is valid
Because while loops cannot read from Scanner
questions.explanation: Validating user input naturally requires reading input at least once before evaluating if it meets criteria.

questions.prompt: What happens if you accidentally write a semicolon after a while loop header: `while (x > 0);`?
options: It causes an infinite loop if x > 0 because the empty statement repeats endlessly
It prints a warning in terminal
questions.explanation: The semicolon becomes the empty loop body. Since x is never updated, x > 0 stays true forever, hanging the thread in an infinite loop.
Pass 1: num = 100 / 2 = 50. Condition 50 > 20 is true. Pass 2: num = 50 / 2 = 25. Condition 25 > 20 is true. Pass 3: num = 25 / 2 = 12. Condition 12 > 20 is false. Output: 12.

questions.prompt: When is a while loop strictly preferred over a for loop?
options: When iterating through an array from start to end
When the termination condition depends on runtime events or states with an unknown iteration count
questions.explanation: When the number of iterations depends on non-deterministic conditions (e.g. user input, stream EOF, state flags), `while` is the natural idiomatic choice.

practice.problemStatement:

Initialize `int userSelection = 3;` (representing Exit).
Inside the do-while body, print:

2. Withdraw
3. Exit

interviewQA.question: What is the fundamental difference between while and do-while loops in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The fundamental difference is the timing of condition evaluation. A `while` loop is a pre-test loop that verifies the condition before entering the body, allowing 0 minimum executions. A `do-while` loop is a post-test loop that verifies the condition after the body finishes, guaranteeing at least 1 execution.
keyPoints: Always state: pre-test vs post-test, and 0 vs 1 minimum iterations.

interviewQA.question: Why is the semicolon mandatory after `while (condition);` in do-while, but forbidden in a standard while loop?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In `do-while`, the `while (condition);` is the end of the entire `do-while` statement, so Java grammar requires a semicolon to terminate the statement. In a normal `while (condition) { ... }`, the while header is immediately followed by a block statement `{ ... }`; placing a semicolon right after the header creates an empty body statement, disconnecting the block that follows.
keyPoints: Explain how statement termination works in Java grammar.

interviewQA.question: How do you implement an event-driven game loop using while in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A game loop typically uses a boolean flag: `boolean isGameOver = false; while (!isGameOver) { processInput(); updateGameState(); render(); }`. When the player dies or chooses to quit, `isGameOver` is set to `true`, cleanly terminating the loop on the next pass.
keyPoints: Mention state flags and game loop architectures.

interviewQA.question: What is a Sentinel-Controlled Loop?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A sentinel-controlled loop is a loop that continues processing inputs until a special predefined 'sentinel' value (such as `-1` or `"exit"`) is entered by the user to signal termination. It is commonly implemented with a `while` loop.
keyPoints: Use the term 'sentinel value' — interviewers recognize it as standard computer science terminology.

interviewQA.question: What is the risk of updating a loop variable at the very end of a complex while block?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: If the loop contains `continue` statements or early error branches that bypass the bottom of the body, the update step will be skipped, causing an accidental infinite loop. In such cases, `for` loops are safer because the update expression is guaranteed to run after every iteration, even when `continue` is invoked.
keyPoints: Highlight the continue-update hazard in while loops.

interviewQA.question: Can variables declared inside a `do` block be used in the `while` condition at the bottom?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No! Variables declared inside the `do { ... }` block have local block scope limited to the curly braces. They are out of scope and cannot be referenced in the trailing `while (condition);`. Any variable used in the condition must be declared before the `do` block.
keyPoints: This is a classic tricky Java syntax question — emphasize lexical scope boundaries.

interviewQA.question: How does compiler optimization handle `while(false)` vs `if(false)`?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `while (false) { ... }` causes a compile-time error: 'unreachable code', because the Java compiler knows the body can never execute. Interestingly, `if (false) { ... }` is permitted by the compiler to allow conditional compilation flags without failing compilation.
keyPoints: Contrast JLS unreachable code rules for while(false) vs if(false).

practiceProblems.description:
Declare `int score = 0;`. Using a do-while loop, print: `Attempt registered: score = 0`, then increment score by 10. Set the condition to `while (score < 0)`. Verify it runs once.

Loop terminated with score: 10

Loop terminated with score: 10

practiceProblems.title: Problem 3: Sum Until Threshold
practiceProblems.description:
Starting with `sum = 0` and `term = 1`, use a while loop to add consecutive integers until `sum >= 20`. Print the final sum and term count:
Final Sum: 21
Terms Added: 6
practiceProblems.hint: while (sum < 20) { sum += term; term++; } (terms added will be term - 1)

practiceProblems.title: Problem 4: PIN Validation Simulator
practiceProblems.description:
Simulate PIN validation where `int attempt = 1; int enteredPin = 1234; int correctPin = 9999;`.
In each attempt of a while loop (up to 3 attempts), print:
Attempt 1: Incorrect PIN
Attempt 2: Incorrect PIN
Attempt 3: Incorrect PIN
Card Blocked: Maximum attempts reached!
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Attempt 1: Incorrect PIN
Attempt 2: Incorrect PIN
Attempt 3: Incorrect PIN
Card Blocked: Maximum attempts reached!
practiceProblems.hint: while (attempt <= 3) { System.out.println("Attempt " + attempt + ": Incorrect PIN"); attempt++; }

practiceProblems.title: Problem 6: Loan Balance Repayment Schedule
practiceProblems.description:
A loan starts at $150. In each monthly cycle of a while loop, $40 is paid off until the balance is 0 or less. Print:
Month 1: Balance remaining $110
Month 2: Balance remaining $70
Month 3: Balance remaining $30
Month 4: Loan fully cleared!
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Month 1: Balance remaining $110
Month 2: Balance remaining $70
Month 3: Balance remaining $30
Month 4: Loan fully cleared!
practiceProblems.hint: int month = 1; while (balance > 0) { balance -= 40; if (balance > 0) print remaining else print cleared; month++; }
